questions.q: On a GitHub repository page, where do you find the URL to clone it?
questions.explain: The Code button shows the HTTPS (and SSH) URL to use with git clone, and a Download ZIP option.

questions.q: What does starring a repository do?
questions.explain: A star is a bookmark and a sign of popularity. Copying to your account is a fork.

questions.q: You will push an existing project from your laptop. How should you create the GitHub repository?
questions.explain: An empty repository avoids 'unrelated histories'. Add a README only when you will clone the new repository.

questions.q: How does a teammate get permission to push to your repository?
questions.explain: Add them as a collaborator; they accept the invitation. Never share your password.

questions.q: Which belong in a good bug report (issue)? (Choose all that apply.)
questions.explain: A good issue lets anyone reproduce the problem. Screenshots and error messages help too.

questions.q: This commit reaches main on GitHub. What happens to issue #3?
questions.code:
$ git commit -m "Fix cart total for repeated items (fixes #3)"
$ git push
questions.explain: Keywords like fixes, closes or resolves followed by an issue number close it when the commit reaches the default branch.

options: A request to review a branch and merge it into another branch
A way to download a repository
questions.explain: A PR proposes merging your branch (for example into main). Teammates review the changes before merging.

questions.q: A reviewer asks for changes to your pull request. What do you do?
options: Push new commits to the same branch; the PR updates automatically
Close it and open a new PR
questions.explain: A PR follows its branch. Every push to the branch appears in the PR.

questions.q: Which merge option combines all of a PR's commits into ONE commit on main?
questions.explain: Squash and merge keeps main's history short: one commit per pull request.

questions.q: What is the difference between a fork and a clone?
options: A fork is a copy on GitHub under your account; a clone is a copy on your computer
A fork is on your computer; a clone is on GitHub
questions.explain: You fork on GitHub (button), then clone your fork to your computer.

questions.q: Put the open-source contribution steps in order.
items: Open a pull request to the original
questions.explain: Fork → clone → branch → commit → push → pull request. Add the original as 'upstream' to stay up to date.

questions.q: In a forked project, what does the remote named 'upstream' usually point to?
options: The original repository you forked from
questions.explain: origin = your fork (you can push); upstream = the original (you pull updates from it).
